# X.509 validity fixtures

Seven DER certificates whose only interesting property is the encoding of their
two validity fields. They are read by `../validity_times.rs`, which is the
evidence that `neotales-x509` reads both ASN.1 time types a validity field can
hold: the two-digit-year `UTCTime` of 1950 through 2049, and the four-digit-year
`GeneralizedTime` that RFC 5280 §4.1.2.5 requires from 2050 on and that a
two-digit year cannot replace before 1950.

They are committed rather than generated at test time so the suite needs neither
a network nor a local `openssl`, and they are generated by the reference
implementation rather than by the crate under test, so they prove something
about X.509 rather than about this crate.

## Generated by

**OpenSSL 3.6.3** (`openssl version` on the machine that generated them, Linux
x86-64). One key for all seven, an Ed25519 key generated fresh:

```sh
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out k.pem
```

Each certificate is a self-signed `req -new -x509` with serial 7, the key
identifier extension OpenSSL adds by default, and the two dates below:

```sh
openssl req -new -x509 -key k.pem -out c.der -outform DER \
    -not_before <notBefore> -not_after <notAfter> \
    -subj /CN=validity-<case>.example -set_serial 7
```

`-not_before` and `-not_after` take `CCYYMMDDHHMMSSZ` and override the usual
`-days`. OpenSSL chooses `UTCTime` or `GeneralizedTime` itself, which is the
point of generating these here rather than by hand: the encoding under test is
the one the reference tool picked for the date.

`k.pem` is deliberately not committed. Nothing verifies these certificates —
the conversion reads the public key and the two times and does not check the
signature — so a committed key would be a secret-shaped file with no use.

## The fixtures

| File | `notBefore` | `notAfter` | Encoding the tool chose | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `validity-1949.der` | 1949-09-28 | 1949-11-27 | `GeneralizedTime` ×2 | Before the `UTCTime` window |
| `validity-1950.der` | 1950-09-28 | 1950-11-27 | `UTCTime` ×2 | First year of the `UTCTime` window |
| `validity-2045.der` | 2045-09-28 | 2045-11-27 | `UTCTime` ×2 | The control: the path that already worked |
| `validity-2049.der` | 2049-09-28 | 2049-11-27 | `UTCTime` ×2 | Last year of the `UTCTime` window |
| `validity-2050.der` | 2050-09-28 | 2050-11-27 | `GeneralizedTime` ×2 | First year the long form is required for |
| `validity-not-after-2136.der` | 2026-09-28 | 2136-11-27 | `UTCTime`, then `GeneralizedTime` | A 110-year certificate, one field of each kind |
| `validity-not-before-1949.der` | 1949-09-28 | 2136-11-27 | `GeneralizedTime` ×2 | A pre-1950 `notBefore` |

Every time is at midnight Zulu, so a timestamp in a test is a whole number of
days rather than something with an hour in it that has to be checked.

`openssl asn1parse -inform DER -in <file>` prints the two encodings, which is how
the table above was checked. `../validity_times.rs` re-checks the encoding from
the bytes before it attempts a conversion, so a fixture regenerated with the
wrong dates fails the test rather than quietly ceasing to cover its case.

## The two rejections

The 1949 and 1950 fixtures do not convert, and that is not a defect. An OpenSSH
certificate's `valid_after` and `valid_before` are `u64` seconds since the Unix
epoch, so a validity date before 1970 has no representation. Their years are
read correctly; the instant is what has nowhere to go. The reason is asserted in
the unit tests in `../src/openssh_cert.rs`, which are the only place that can see
it, because the public error is a single variant.
